lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- Numbers That Talk
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- André Gregolin Zanin | Lesson 16 -- Numbers That Talk
lesson.grammar_point: language of data and trends: verb and noun phrases of change, prepositions and approximation

listenings.text: When I started working as an analyst for a basketball team, the coach gave me one rule. Never show me a number without the line behind it. Over the last twenty years, three-point attempts in professional basketball have more than doubled. On its own, that number tells you almost nothing. The line tells you the story. Our own attempts rose steadily for four seasons, reached a peak, and then leveled off. At the same time, our shooting percentage dropped slightly. So the coach asked a better question. Are we shooting more because we are better, or only because everybody else is? The data could not answer that. What it did was make the question sharper, and that is roughly what good data always does.

Most people describe a graph from left to right, one number at a time, and by the third number the listener is lost. Try three steps instead. First, the big picture. Overall, the number of applicants has risen over the last ten years. Second, the biggest change. There was a sharp drop in one year, followed by a steady recovery. Third, one detail that surprised you. And please round your numbers. Nobody remembers forty-seven point three percent. Everybody remembers just under half. Finally, watch two small words. Prices rose by ten percent tells me the difference. Prices rose to ten dollars tells me where they ended. Mix them up, and your listener gets the wrong story from the right numbers.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to go up and down again and again
less than half of a group of people or things
to be a particular part or amount of a total
a general direction in which something is changing over time
to stop rising or falling and stay at about the same level
the highest point or level that something reaches
a part of a group or an amount, compared with the whole
close to the real number, but not exact
more than half of a group of people or things

paras: Every December, Marta Ribeiro, the coordinator of a cursinho in São Paulo, publishes a one-page report on the year in numbers. This year, 412 students took part, and the majority were aiming at medicine. In fact, medicine students accounted for just under half of the whole group. Marta expected the report to show a simple trend: more study, better results. The data told a different story.

The first line in the report is study hours. In February, students reported studying roughly forty hours a week. The number rose steadily until June, when it reached a peak of just over sixty hours a week. After the July break, it fluctuated between fifty and fifty-five hours, and it stayed there until November.

The second line is mock exam scores. There was a sharp rise in mock exam scores in the first three months, when hours were still low. From June onwards, however, scores leveled off, even though hours were at their highest. Students who slept fewer than six hours a night accounted for nearly a third of the group, and only a small minority of them improved after June. “More hours did not mean more points,” Marta writes.

The last number is the one that worries her most. Burnout is on the rise: the proportion of students who felt exhausted has doubled since last year. Her advice for next year is short. Approximate numbers are fine, she says, but read the line, not the single number. “A number on its own is a fact. A line is a story.”
reading.source: A composite cursinho year-end report, written for this lesson. The numbers are illustrative.

choices: To show that a year of numbers can tell a story that a single number hides.
To prove that students who study more than sixty hours a week always get the highest scores in their mock exams.
To explain how a cursinho chooses its students.

items: Most of the students in the report were aiming at medicine.
The majority were aiming at medicine.
Study hours reached a peak in February.
They reached a peak in June, at just over sixty hours a week.
After the July break, study hours fell steadily until November.
They fluctuated between fifty and fifty-five hours, and stayed there.
Scores rose sharply when study hours were still low.
There was a sharp rise in mock exam scores in the first three months, when hours were still low.
The majority of the students slept fewer than six hours a night.
They accounted for nearly a third of the group, not the majority.
The proportion of exhausted students is twice as high as last year.
The proportion of students who felt exhausted has doubled since last year.

items.situation: Describe how your study hours have changed since the start of the year, with a verb and an adverb.
tips: My study hours have risen considerably since February.
Since + up to now = present perfect.

items.situation: Say the same change with an adjective and a noun: My scores rose sharply.
tips: There was a sharp rise in my scores.
Before a noun, an adjective: sharp, not sharply.

items.situation: Round this number naturally: 47.3% of the class sleeps less than seven hours.
tips: Just under half of the class sleeps less than seven hours.
Nobody remembers 47.3. Everybody remembers just under half.

items.situation: Your basketball training went from 10 to 25 hours a week in one year. Say it with from and to.
tips: My training went from ten to twenty-five hours a week.
From the start point, to the end point.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: The price of the cursinho increased in fifteen percent.
tips: The price of the cursinho increased by fifteen percent.
The difference takes by, never in.

items.situation: Describe something in your life that went up and down all year.
tips: My motivation fluctuated all year, but it never disappeared.
Up and down, again and again: fluctuate.
